title: Biomechanical Analysis of the Cross, Hook, and Uppercut in Junior vs. Elite Boxers: Implications for Training and Talent Identification
journal_or_venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
retraction_or_correction_status: no retraction or correction recorded in OpenAlex at accessed_at
notes: cited_by_count 43 at harvest; a citation count is a measure of attention, not of correctness
methodology: 17-unit inertial measurement suit; standardised maximal cross, hook and uppercut; elite versus junior comparison of velocity, stability, force and joint contribution.
main_findings: Elite boxers produced more force at higher velocity than juniors on all three punch types - the gap is not one punch, it is the whole set.
Juniors leaned more on the shoulder; the difference between levels is where the punch comes from, not how hard the arm is thrown.
A front-versus-rear ground reaction force imbalance appeared in the cross only, in both groups.
limitations: standardised punches on command, not chosen in an exchange
IMU-derived force rather than direct force-plate impact

quoted_evidence.quote: Juniors presenting a higher contribution of the shoulder for the three punch types

project_implications: Skill differences in canon are currently expressed as attributes that scale output. This says the real difference is which segments contribute - a shape difference, not a multiplier.
If a fighter profile ever wants to model "trained", the honest handle is the kinetic chain, not a damage number.
